headline: Great Point Boils With Bass and Blues — Bonito Still a Rumor, But Not for Long
subhead: Bunker got pushed into the rip this week and the stripers under them didn't need an invitation — meanwhile Block Island's warming fast enough to make me nervous about missing the first bonito.
body_markdown:
Wednesday morning, first light, I'm sitting off Great Point watching a bait ball get worked from both ends — terns dropping on it from above, something big boiling it from below, and for about four seconds I let myself believe it was albies. It wasn't. Pulled a bluefish out of that mess on the first cast, a good one too, mid-teens, and then a 28-inch bass right behind it on the next drift. So no albies yet. But I'll tell you what — that's the kind of scene that's going to have albies in it soon, and every rip chaser on this island is circling the calendar the same way I am.

Let's start with what's actually happening, because it's been a decent week and I don't want to bury it under bonito talk. The bunker have been thick off the Point and down along Coskata, pushed tight to the beach by the current, and the bass have settled into a very predictable pattern around them — first light and last light, right on the edge of the rip where the sandy bottom drops into that deeper channel. I've been running bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet, letting it sit on bottom during the last of the ebb, and it's produced fish from 28 inches up to a couple that pushed 40. Nothing crazy, but honest work, and the kind of bite you can set a schedule around. Daytime, with the sun up and the water warming, those same fish go quiet — that's the pattern right now south of the Cape, warm shallow water pushing the keeper-class stripers nocturnal, and Nantucket Sound is no exception. If you want bass in daylight, fish the deeper edges of Nantucket Shoals where there's some current relief, or wait for dusk.

Bluefish have been the more reliable daylight fish, and they've been genuinely fun — packs of them working bunker schools along the Sound side beaches from Cape Poge Gut to Sankaty, visible from shore some mornings if you're paying attention to the birds. Poppers and metal — I've had good luck with a 2-ounce Hammered Kastmaster — worked through the edges of the blitz without needing to be in the thick of the froth. This bluefish push has legs; the weather's been stable, bait's staying put, and as long as we don't get a wind event that scatters everything, I'd expect this to keep going and maybe spread further into the Sound over the next week or two.

Fluke's been the quiet workhorse all month, and it hasn't slowed a bit. Nantucket Shoals is still the money spot — that structure holds bottom bait all summer regardless of what the surface water's doing, and I've been drifting the edges in 25 to 35 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance. Best window has been the two hours around the tide change, either way, when the drift slows enough to keep the bait in the strike zone instead of skipping across it. Legal fish have been steady, a few pushing 6 pounds, and scup mixed in on the same drifts for anyone who wants a fish fry.

Now the bonito watch — because I know that's what half of you are actually reading this for. Nothing confirmed in the Sound yet. But we flagged this a few days back when Block Island's water crossed into that comfort range for bonito, and said to expect it moving east through the Sound over the next week to ten days. I'm not backing off that call. The water's been climbing steadily, the bait's here, and every year it's the same script — bonito show up quiet, usually first spotted as a fast, tight-schooled disturbance that looks nothing like a bluefish blitz, way out on the edge of the rip where you almost don't notice it. I'll be running out to the Shoals and Great Point at first light every chance I get from here through the end of the month with a Deadly Dick rigged and ready, because when they show, the window to be in the right spot is short.

Monomoy's been more of a grind. The SW wind we've had on and off has kept the rips there working, but the fishing's been mixed — good stretches of bass on the drop of the tide around the elbow, then nothing for an hour, then a flurry again. If I had to guess why, it's the current getting softened up as we slide toward Tuesday's first-quarter neap — less water moving through those rips means the bait isn't getting pinned as hard, and the fish get spread out instead of stacked. I'd still fish it, just don't expect the kind of concentrated bite you get on a bigger tide. Eels at dusk have been the better call down there over bucktails right now.

Looking ahead — the softer tides through the neap should widen the productive window at spots like Great Point and the Monomoy rips beyond just the peak of the flow, which is good news if your schedule doesn't line up perfectly with the moon. I'd keep working bass on bunker at dawn and dusk, keep the popper rod rigged for blues in daylight, and keep one eye permanently on the horizon for that first bonito flash. It's close. I can feel it.
